newsitem.title: USA: Dole attacks Clinton on immigration, affirmative action.
newsitem.headline: Dole attacks Clinton on immigration, affirmative action.

text.p: Republican presidential nominee Bob Dole attacked President Bill Clinton and emphasised the emotional issues of immigration and affirmative action on Sunday as he made an all-out effort to win this key state.

A fired-up Dole complained that Americans ought to be "fed up to their eyeballs" with Clinton and tried to suggest the president faced ethics charges so serious he might not serve out his second term.

At a sun-drenched rally of Vietnamese-Americans, Dole criticised Clinton for not doing enough to police California's borders and underlined his support for a controversial ballot initiative to end affirmative action in state hiring, contracting and school admissions.

"There are no limits on what individuals can achieve in this country when they come here as legal immigrants. Because in America what counts is merit and character," Dole said, standing before a red, white and blue banner that read "Celebrating Legal Immigration, the American Dream."
"Quotas, set asides and other preferences that discriminate by race or ethnicity are simply wrong in America ... and do violence to the principles of our Constitution," Dole said.
Clinton opposes the affirmative action initiative.

Later, at a Republican steak and oyster feed in Elk Grove, Dole referred to comments Reform Party candidate Ross Perot made on NBC's "Meet the Press" suggesting Clinton and first lady Hillary Rodham Clinton would face serious ethics charges in a second term.

"Then again, Ross Perot suggests that it may not be four more years. Maybe it's going to be so serious next year somebody might be in real trouble. I did not say that, Ross Perot did. But I've thought about it, I've thought about it," Dole said.
Dole later denied he was saying Clinton would be impeached.
With only nine days until the election, Dole is focusing much of his dwindling time and millions of dollars in advertising in this key state. The majority are tough ads on immigration.
In a sign he intends an all-out effort, Dole extended his California campaign swing one day until Tuesday.
But a recent Los Angeles Times poll shows Dole trailing Clinton by 20 percentage points in California, which has 54 of the 270 electoral college votes needed to win the White House.
Dole was acid in complaining about Craig Livingstone, a former aide and one-time bar bouncer who left the White House after ordering FBI files on Republicans.
"They've turned the White House into something else. It's the animal house," Dole said, complaining Americans should be fed "up to their eyeballs" with the administration.
He slammed the New York Times for endorsing Clinton Sunday, calling the paper an arm of the Democratic National Committee and an "apologist" for the White House.
Dole, who tried unsuccessfully to persuade Perot to quit the race, called on Perot backers to support him and said he was pleased by the Texas billionaire's suggestion he would be a better leader.

Perot said on "Meet the Press" that "Senator Dole understands combat. He has certainly paid a terrible price, and if you were limited to those two, you'd certainly, I think every American would pick him, because he understands what he's doing."
Despite his decision to go on the attack on illegal immigration, Dole showed some political sensitivity about the issue in his speech to the ethnic crowd in San Jose.
He did not repeat his usual call to bar non-citizens from voting or his accusation that the Clinton administration was speeding up citizenship applicants of legal immigrants.
California voters by a wide margin passed an initiative to bar most benefits to illegal immigrants, but it has been held up by the courts.
